item.title: What Equity Prop Desk Traders Should Actually Track (It Isn't Win Rate)
item.description: A +$4,100 month where four transport names made +$12,600 and everything else lost $8,500 is not a good month, it is one sector call. The desk metric set: attribution, return on deployed capital, correlated clusters, borrow cost.
item.content:encoded: Retail metrics answer a personal question - is this working, should I keep doing it. Desk metrics answer an allocation question - what should this trader be given next quarter, and what is the risk of giving it. Three things follow: net P&L stops being the headline because on its own it cannot separate a repeatable edge from one good sector call, capital becomes a denominator rather than a background fact, and positions stop being independent because a book is a set of exposures, several of which are usually the same exposure wearing different tickers. Win rate survives none of it, saying nothing about size, capital consumed, or whether the winners and losers were the same bet. The attribution section works a month that closes at +$4,100 and looks unremarkable until it is decomposed by name: UNP +$5,200, NSC +$3,100, CSX +$2,400 and ODFL +$1,900 against MSFT +$700, PFE -$4,300 and KO -$4,900. The four transport names produced +$12,600 while everything else lost $8,500, so this was not a +$4,100 month, it was one correct sector call carrying a book that was otherwise bleeding, and the net figure is the only presentation that hides it. Three attribution axes are recommended: by name (the outlier-concentration test that decides whether an edge is real or three lucky trades), by sector (the equities-specific axis with no forex equivalent, which turns seven trades into two decisions), and by catalyst - earnings, guidance, M&A, index events, macro prints, pure technicals - the axis nobody logs and the one that most reliably explains why a strategy stops working, because catalysts come in regimes. Return on capital deployed is then set out as the number that separates two traders the P&L report calls identical: both finish at +$40,000, but one averaged $2,000,000 of deployed capital for a 2.0 percent return and the other averaged $600,000 for 6.7 percent, more than three times apart on the metric that decides who gets the next dollar of buying power. Two implementation details are stressed - average deployed capital must be time-weighted rather than taken from peak or month-end, since a position held two days does not consume what one held three weeks does, and it should measure capital actually tied up rather than the allocation on paper, because the gap between the two is itself the finding. The habit it disciplines is parking size in low-conviction positions that neither lose money nor earn their keep. Concentration gets the longest treatment because it is the measurement gap that most separates a desk book from a retail one. UNP, NSC and CSX are railroads and ODFL is trucking, so four positions each sized at 1 percent of the book leave a trader who believes they carry 1 percent per idea in fact carrying roughly 4 percent on a single question about freight volumes. It worked, which is why nobody looked; the month it does not work, three or four stops resolve on the same morning. Position-count risk rules are blind to this: no more than six open positions and no more than 2 percent per name are both satisfied by a book that is one bet, so what is needed is exposure grouped into correlated clusters with risk summed inside each cluster rather than across the position list. Long/short books get a subtler version - long four industrials against short two staples is not market neutral, it is a single cyclical-versus-defensive factor bet with a beta that appears nowhere in the position list, and netting gross exposure to something small does not make a book neutral, it makes the factor concentration harder to see. The useful form of the question is pre-trade rather than monthly: does the order I am about to send join a cluster that is already heavy, asked while the size is still editable. Borrow and locate are then argued as per-trade fields rather than a monthly financing line nobody attributes, with the arithmetic spelled out: a $100,000 short held 21 days at a 40 percent annualized rate costs $2,301, so if the average winning short makes $3,000 gross, borrow has taken roughly three quarters of the edge and a journal recording only entry and exit price will never show it. Rates are hedged honestly as ranging from a few basis points to triple digits annualized, moving daily and differing between prime brokers, so the figure is an example rather than a benchmark. Three fields close the gap - borrow rate at entry, the general-collateral or hard-to-borrow flag, and accrued financing at exit - after which the common finding that the hard-to-borrow subset has worse net expectancy despite better gross numbers becomes visible. On execution the piece is careful about what is actually computable: arrival price and interval VWAP are what real desks use and both need a market data feed alongside the fills, which is why they live in a firm's execution stack rather than any journal. Benchmarked slippage asks whether your execution was good relative to what the market offered; trigger-based slippage, the difference between your fill and the price your own order was supposed to trigger at, asks whether your plan survived contact, needs no market data, and for a discretionary trader is arguably more actionable - it catches stops filling three cents through on thin names and limit orders that never get the price you assumed when you sized. MAE and MFE sit alongside, with the highest-value intraday cut being MAE by liquidity band: consistently deeper adverse excursion on thinner names means the stop is placed against a spread rather than an invalidation level, and the fix is sizing rather than a tighter stop. A full section is given to when the firm's own system already does all of this, on the grounds that a desk risk stack sitting on the fills and the market data in real time is better at it than any journal, quoting an equity trader who described his firm as running its own trading terminal and its own accounting and metrics, a closed ecosystem. The test offered is concrete: if you can already answer from existing screens what your return on deployed capital was last month and which correlated cluster produced your largest drawdown, stop there. The three cases where an individual record still earns its place are a system that reports position and risk but never decision quality, portability since a track record living in an employer's database does not travel when you do, and traders running a personal book alongside a desk seat. Closes on what SignalDeck actually does: the pre-trade concentration check is built in and runs before the order, grouping the open equity book into correlated clusters by sector resolved automatically from the ticker's SIC classification rather than self-labelled, flagging a prospective position that joins an already-heavy cluster with combined dollar, R and percent-of-account exposure, with UNP and NSC as the worked example and unresolvable tickers counting toward total open risk while joining no cluster. MAE/MFE, trigger-based execution metrics, per-strategy aggregation and the R, expectancy, SQN and Monte Carlo layer are present. Four gaps are stated plainly: sector is not stored on a trade so there is no historical P&L-by-sector report, there is no return-on-capital-deployed metric, there are no borrow or financing fields, and execution is benchmarked against your own trigger and never against arrival price or VWAP because no market data feed is ingested alongside fills.

item.title: Running Three Funded Accounts and a Personal One: How to Journal Multiple Accounts Without Losing the Plot
item.description: Four accounts at +3,200, +1,400, -1,900 and +800 sum to a healthy +3,500 month - and hide the evaluation that was already dead at -1,200. P&L is additive. Risk headroom is not.
item.content:encoded: Multi-account trading is now the default shape of a serious retail career - pass an evaluation, add a second firm to spread payout risk, keep a personal account for the setups the firms restrict - and the measurement layer is what breaks first, because almost every journal treats the account as a label rather than as a boundary. The piece opens on a month that looks fine: four accounts returning +3,200, +1,400, -1,900 and +800 for a blended +3,500, where the -1,900 sat on a 20,000 dollar evaluation with a static 6 percent maximum loss. That account was gone at -1,200 and then kept trading in the trader's spreadsheet for another 700 dollars the firm had already stopped counting. The structural reason is that P&L is additive and risk headroom is not: every account's meaningful risk number is its own remaining distance to its own limit, denominated against a different balance under different rules, and no arithmetic combines those into a portfolio figure because there is no shared limit for the combination to be measured against. The fix is not four separate journals, which fragments the sample exactly where it needs to be whole - a setup traded 40 times across four accounts is one sample of 40, not four samples of ten - so you need two readings of one dataset: an account-scoped view for risk (equity curve, current and maximum drawdown, distance to limit, reset clock, payout progress, always one account at a time and never summed) and a strategy-scoped view for edge (expectancy, profit factor, SQN, win rate by setup and session, always pooled and only ever in R). Dollars do not survive the pooling: a 50,000 dollar account risking 1 percent has a 500 dollar R and a 150,000 dollar account risking 0.5 percent has a 750 dollar R, so the same +2R trade pays 1,000 against 1,500 and the larger account looks 50 percent better while both trades performed identically. Once everything is in R a second diagnostic appears: if one setup averages +0.42R on one account and +0.11R on another, that gap is not edge, it is execution - fills, spreads, copier latency or a rounded lot size. On correlation, four accounts taking the same signals are one position expressed four times, correlation approximately 1.0 by construction. If a single account has a 65 percent chance of reaching payout, four independent accounts would average 2.6 survivors with a standard deviation near 0.95; four perfectly correlated accounts average the same 2.6 with a standard deviation near 1.91, because the real distribution is barbell shaped - 65 percent of the time all four survive and 35 percent of the time none do. The expected value is unchanged and the spread scales with the square root of the account count, which makes stacking accounts a leverage decision rather than a diversification one. A rule-tracking table covers what actually differs between rulebooks (drawdown model, drawdown basis, daily loss limit and reset timezone, consistency rules, payout threshold and split, instrument and news restrictions), all hedged as categories to verify against each firm's current rulebook rather than claims about any firm. The copy-trading section covers per-broker slippage and spread, copier latency, commission and swap schedules, and the lot-rounding trap: a 0.03 lot position on a 100K account scaled to a 20K account should be 0.006 lots, but the 0.01 minimum rounds it up, so that account carries 67 percent more risk than intended on every trade, permanently - which is why each account's own fills must be imported rather than the master's records relabelled. Scaling gets an arithmetic test: expected fee cost per funded account is the evaluation fee divided by your realistic pass rate, so a 250 dollar evaluation at a 40 percent pass rate costs about 625 dollars in expected fees before it earns anything, and if that does not clear what a funded account returns per month after the split times its typical survival, the account is a subscription rather than an investment. Monte Carlo modelling gets a correction: resample one trade sequence and apply it to all four accounts with each account's own size and rules, rather than simulating four independent accounts, which quietly assumes diversification that does not exist. Closes with the fields to log (account per trade set at import, cash at risk on that account, firm and account configuration, signal price against actual fill, realized lot size after rounding, strategy tag) and an honest account of what SignalDeck does here: two account dimensions per trade (broker created per connection, plus a user-named funding account), a nav account selector that scopes dashboard stats, calendar, year heatmap and exports, and per-connection balances used for risk percentage on MetaTrader imports - alongside two stated limits, that the risk profile is currently a single user-level setting rather than one per funding account, and that SignalDeck does not encode each firm's specific drawdown rule, so the firm's own dashboard remains the authoritative number for headroom.

item.title: Journaling XAUUSD: Why Gold Distorts Your R-Multiples and How to Normalize It
item.description: A 50 pip stop on gold can mean $50 or $5,000 of real risk depending on whose pip definition your broker uses. How to size XAUUSD from the contract spec and normalize gold to R so it is comparable to everything else you trade.
item.content:encoded: Most journaling advice written for forex quietly assumes every instrument behaves like EURUSD: a stable contract size, an unambiguous pip, a spread you can treat as a rounding error. Gold breaks all three, and the result is a journal where XAUUSD trades are not on the same scale as anything else in it. The piece starts with what actually differs. XAUUSD looks like a currency pair but is a commodity contract quoted in dollars per troy ounce, with specifications set per broker rather than by market convention; a standard lot is commonly 100 troy ounces, which makes a $1.00 price move worth $100 per lot, and that number lives in the broker contract specification rather than in the instrument name. Then the pip problem: the term was borrowed from currency trading and never given a fixed meaning on metals, so one pip on gold is variously quoted as $0.01, $0.10 or $1.00. On a 100 ounce lot those are worth $1, $10 and $100 respectively, so the same instruction to risk a 50 pip stop on one lot costs $50 under one convention and $5,000 under another. That is a hundredfold range in real risk produced entirely by a word, and every R multiple derived from a mis-sized position inherits the same error. The fix is not to settle which definition is correct, since there is no authority to appeal to, but to stop using pips on gold and size directly from the contract spec: lots equals cash risk divided by stop distance in price times contract size, so a $500 risk with a $4.00 stop on a 100 ounce contract gives exactly 1.25 lots with no pip appearing anywhere. Spread gets treated as a logged line item rather than a rounding error, because what matters is the ratio of spread to stop: a $0.50 spread against a $4.00 stop consumes 12.5% of 1R at entry, but against a scalper's $1.00 stop it consumes 50% of 1R, so the trade must travel half the risk budget just to reach break even. Since gold spreads widen at rollover, around scheduled data and in thin overnight liquidity, the advice is to log signal price against realized fill price per trade and track the distribution rather than the average, because the cost concentrates in a tail. A worked example then puts a XAUUSD scalp and a EURUSD swing on one axis at the same $500 risk: the gold trade sizes to 1.25 lots and returns $1,500, the currency trade sizes to 1.67 lots and returns about $1,000, which in cash looks like gold winning by 50% but in R is a clean 3.0R against 2.0R, a statement about the setups rather than about contract specifications. Also covers session segmentation, since gold has a structure currency pairs do not share, anchored by the twice daily LBMA Gold Price auctions at 10:30 and 15:00 London time plus the New York open, and an aggregate gold statistic usually hides two or three distributions stacked on each other, with the common finding being that one session carries the whole edge while the others quietly consume it. MAE gets a section because tight stops plus variable spread create a failure mode no other metric separates: losers clustering at 1.0R to 1.3R before the price recovers means you are being stopped by noise and spread rather than by invalidation, and the usual response of tightening the stop further accelerates the problem. Closes with the prop firm metals provisions worth verifying before a challenge rather than after a violation, all of which vary by firm and change, and the specific fields to log so any of this is answerable later: contract size and broker per trade, stop distance in price units rather than pips, signal and realized fill price, a session tag, and MAE and MFE recorded in R.

item.title: Your Backtest Said 2.1 SQN and Live Says 0.6: Diagnosing Backtest-to-Live Divergence
item.description: A 2.1 SQN backtest and a 0.6 SQN live run might just be a small sample, not two different strategies. How to rule out variance, then rank the six real causes - slippage, commissions, look-ahead bias, data quality, regime change, latency.
item.content:encoded: A backtest cleared every filter - 2,000 trades, a System Quality Number north of 2, a clean equity curve. Three months live, the same rules are producing 0.6. That gap does not by itself say whether the strategy is broken, the backtest was wrong, or the live sample is simply too small yet to say anything. The piece works through it in order. First, rule out variance: the standard error of a mean shrinks with the square root of sample size, not linearly, so a 40-trade live sample carries roughly seven times the standard error of a 2,000-trade backtest - a live SQN that looks dramatically worse can still sit inside that wider confidence interval. If the sample has grown past a hundred or so trades and the intervals still do not overlap, it moves to the six real causes, ranked by how often they are the culprit: slippage and spread the backtest under-modeled, commission modeling that was flat-rated or missing, look-ahead bias using information not available at decision time, survivorship and data quality problems in the historical feed, genuine regime change, and execution latency between signal and fill - the last two are the hardest to prove and the ones reached for first out of convenience. Covers measuring actual slippage by logging expected fill against realized fill on every trade and feeding the measured distribution back into the backtest's cost model; the overfitting tell, where an in-sample-only backtest with no walk-forward validation is not a mystery to diagnose but the out-of-sample test arriving three months late; distinguishing regime change from a broken strategy with rolling expectancy against the lifetime figure, and why the correct response is opposite (reduce size and wait vs. stop and rebuild); the reconciliation loop of re-running the backtest with measured live costs and comparing corrected curves within a statistical tolerance band; and the five fields worth logging now - expected vs. actual fill price, latency, real commission per trade, and a strategy tag linking every live trade back to its backtest version - so the next divergence is answerable in minutes instead of requiring this whole forensic process again.

item.title: Why Your Prop Firm Dashboard and Your Journal Disagree (and Which One to Trust)
item.description: Your journal says +$1,240 and the firm's dashboard says +$928. Five reasons the two disagree - commissions, swap, open P&L, the reset clock, partial fills - and a ten minute tie-out that closes the $312 gap.
item.content:encoded: You are mid evaluation. Your journal says you are up $1,240 on the day with plenty of daily loss budget left, and the firm's dashboard says $928 and a smaller cushion than you expected. One of those numbers decides whether you still have an account tomorrow, and it is not the one you keep. A discrepancy between a journal and a prop firm dashboard is almost never a mystery and almost never the firm making an error: it decomposes into five specific causes that stack, which is why it rarely resolves on the first guess. Commissions and fees, when the journal recorded gross prices. Swap, financing or carry on anything held past the rollover. Unrealized P&L on open positions, which the firm counts in equity and a closed trade journal ignores entirely. The firm's daily reset landing on its clock rather than yours, so a trade at 17:05 New York can be charged to a day that has barely started. And partial or rejected fills, where you journaled the size you intended instead of the size you got. The piece separates the three numbers most dashboards display at once - balance, equity, and the trailing threshold - and makes the point that if you cannot say from memory whether your firm's high water mark is set on balance or on equity, you do not currently know what your worst case trade costs you. It covers the timezone trap in detail, including the daylight saving drift between a CE(S)T server day and a New York boundary, and why unrealized P&L is the gap that actually ends accounts: a position that runs 3R intraday and comes back to flat is a non event in a closed trade journal, and may have ratcheted a trailing floor up by the full excursion. Then a ten minute reconciliation procedure - align the window on the firm's clock, match trade counts before amounts, walk the adjustment stack in order, record the residual daily - with a worked example that ties $1,240 back to $928 through commissions of $84, swap of $63, a partial fill of $95 and a $70 open position mark. Three of those four lines are permanent journal corrections; the fourth never goes away. Closes with what to do when the numbers still disagree, why the firm's number governs regardless, and the four inputs that produce a headroom figure you can actually trust before you size a trade.

item.title: Trading Your Own Capital: The Metrics That Matter When Nobody Is Enforcing a Drawdown Rule
item.description: A prop firm's drawdown limit is a subsidy, not a constraint - it computes your risk and enforces it whether you feel like it or not. Trading your own money, nothing does. How to build the equivalent yourself.
item.content:encoded: Most journaling advice is written for funded traders, because prop firms hand writers a convenient villain: a hard drawdown limit with a number attached. If the money in the account is yours, none of that applies, and nearly every article on this blog frames the value of a journal around a rule you do not have. This one does not. The starting point is that a prop firm's drawdown limit is better understood as a subsidy than a constraint: the firm pays to compute, in real time, how far you are from a loss you cannot come back from, how much of today's budget you have already spent, and whether the trade you are about to open is compatible with both - then enforces the answer without asking your opinion at 2am. Trading your own capital you keep all the upside a funded trader gives away, and you lose the one mechanism that was doing your risk management when you did not feel like doing it. So steal the mechanism, not the rule. The piece covers how to derive a self-imposed drawdown limit that actually binds, using a Monte Carlo resample of your own R-multiples and reading the P10 worst-decile drawdown rather than picking a round number (a worked example shows why a casual "I stop at 10%" rule sits inside a strategy's ordinary variance, fires during a perfectly normal bad stretch, and trains you to override it). It lays out the four metrics that replace "did I pass?" - per-setup expectancy, SQN, rolling-versus-lifetime divergence, and planned-versus-actual risk adherence, the last of which funded traders get policed for free and self-funded traders almost never track. It covers position sizing with fixed-R as the floor and Kelly as a ceiling you should never approach, why sizing off account percentage rather than fixed dollars matters once your balance compounds or takes a withdrawal, the failure mode unique to self-funded traders (nothing stops the 3x size trade at 2am except a mechanical pre-trade gate), and precisely which numbers deposits and withdrawals corrupt: R-multiples survive intact, every percentage-based figure and the raw equity curve do not. Closes with the extra fields worth logging now if you might ever attempt a funded challenge later.

item.title: Which Trading Platforms Can a Journal Actually Sync With?
item.description: Every journal claims broker support, and almost none say what kind. MT4/MT5, Tradovate, Rithmic, NinjaTrader, cTrader, IBKR - what connects live, what needs CSV, and what CSV-only still gives you.
item.content:encoded: Every trading journal's landing page lists analytics features, and almost none are precise about what "syncs with your broker" actually means. There are three connection types on the market and they are not interchangeable: a broker-side API session that sees open positions and live balance, a terminal-side script or EA that only writes closed trades while the terminal runs, and CSV file import that sees everything the export contains but only after the fact. This guide is the honest platform-by-platform matrix. MT4 and MT5 connect live through MetaApi (Elite plan) - no EA, real-time balance sync. Tradovate syncs directly for futures, with one carve-out: many but not all Apex and Topstep evaluation accounts restrict outside API access regardless of the underlying platform, so CSV is the path there instead. NinjaTrader and Rithmic-based setups go through CSV export, with a named NinjaTrader format that handles futures contract multipliers automatically. cTrader connects live via OAuth across any cTrader broker, IBKR connects through the free Flex Web Service, and SnapTrade aggregates 30+ retail brokers. Below that tier - Indian F&O brokers on proprietary dealer terminals, in-house desk platforms with closed accounting stacks - generic CSV is the honest answer, not a dead end. The piece also lays out exactly what CSV-only import still gives you: R-multiples, per-setup expectancy, SQN, and Monte Carlo all run fine on imported history. What it cannot give you is live drawdown headroom while a position is still open, because that requires reading your account's current state, not its history. Closes with a five-question compatibility checklist to run against any vendor before paying for a journal.

item.title: Do You Need a Trading Journal If You Are Already Profitable?
item.description: The most common objection to journaling: I am already profitable without one. Here is an honest answer - what profit alone cannot prove, a 10 minute concentration test for your broker statement, and when skipping it is correct.
item.content:encoded: The most common objection to keeping a trading journal is that it is unnecessary once you are making money, and it usually comes from credible people with real track records. That deserves a real answer rather than a sales pitch. Net profit is an output. It is one number summarising thousands of decisions across one particular sequence of market conditions, and it structurally cannot separate a durable edge from a favourable regime, a broad edge from a handful of outliers, or good sizing from lucky sizing. It also has no derivative: it tells you where you have been, not which way you are moving, which is why a strategy that began decaying six months ago can still show a healthy lifetime figure. Three questions profit alone cannot answer: which of my setups actually makes money, is my edge decaying right now, and how bad can this realistically get. That last one matters most to experienced traders, because your worst observed drawdown is a single sample from a distribution and the typical bad path may be far deeper. Before deciding anything, run the concentration test on data you already have: export your closed trades, sum the net profit, delete the top five winners, and sum the remainder. If what is left is still profitable you have a broad edge with big winners on top. If it is negative, your entire result is five trades. Both profiles report the same headline number and only one is repeatable. The article also covers the four fields that make a log worth keeping (setup tag, result in R, planned versus actual risk, one line of context), the roughly 30 trades per setup you need before drawing conclusions, and the three cases where not journaling is genuinely correct: trading on a desk whose risk system already computes attribution, running a fully systematic live versus backtest pipeline, or trading too infrequently for any sample to mean anything. In all three you already perform the function under a different name.

item.title: Apex Trader Funding Rules Explained: The Trailing Drawdown Trap
item.description: Apex's trailing drawdown follows your intraday high-water mark, then locks - which is why traders blow accounts after a good session, not a bad one. A worked $50K example, plus what your journal must track live.
item.content:encoded: Most traders who blow an Apex Trader Funding account do it right after a good session, not a bad one. The reason is the trailing drawdown - a maximum loss limit that follows your account's intraday high-water mark upward, including unrealized profit on open trades, and then sits there when you give the gains back. Worked $50K example: you spike +$1,800 on an open position, so your peak equity hits $51,800 and the trailing floor climbs with it. You close flat at $50,000 - zero realized profit - yet your loss buffer shrank from $2,500 to $700, because the floor locked in the peak of a trade you round-tripped. That is the mechanic that catches every trader coming from a static-drawdown firm like FTMO, whose overall limit is anchored to the starting balance from day one. The good news is the Apex floor stops trailing once your account gains enough, then becomes static. This guide breaks down the account specs and profit targets, the intraday-peak trailing rule with a full worked example, the Performance Account and payout rules, the three behaviors that cause most blowups, the exact fields your journal must log live (running peak, distance-to-floor in R, peak-to-close giveback), and how to run 1,000 Monte Carlo paths on your own trade history to estimate your pass probability before you pay the fee. Verify all current numbers at apextraderfunding.com - Apex changes its rules often.

item.title: How to Use Monte Carlo to Decide If You Are Ready for a Prop Firm Challenge
item.description: Most traders find out if they were ready by paying the fee and failing. Monte Carlo lets you ask first: resample your own trade history across 1,000 simulated attempts and read your pass probability against the firm's drawdown limit.
item.content:encoded: A prop firm challenge is a bet: pay an evaluation fee, then hit a profit target without breaching a drawdown limit. Most traders find out whether they were ready by failing and reaching for the card again - three attempts at $150 to $600 each is real money spent to reach one funded account (rough estimates, verify current pricing). There is a cheaper way to ask the question. Monte Carlo simulation resamples the sequence of your historical R-multiples across 1,000 or more simulated attempts, keeping your real edge intact and only shuffling the order. Each path is a plausible alternative history of the same strategy, and because a challenge is decided by the path your equity takes - not just where it ends - this is the right lens. Count the paths that reach the target without ever breaching the limit and you have your pass probability. This guide covers the trade history you need (30 to 50 trades, same instrument, R-normalized), how to read pass probability and worst-case P10 drawdown, and the most useful move of all: overlay the firm's limit on your simulated paths and shrink your risk per trade until the breach rate falls. You size to survive the rules, then attempt - free during beta.

item.title: Edgewonk Alternative: Why Prop and Forex Traders Are Switching in 2026
item.description: Edgewonk is now an annual subscription (about $169 to $197/yr); its MT4/MT5 Auto Sync imports closed trades only, with no walk-forward and a what-if simulator, not Monte Carlo on your real trades. A fair 2026 comparison.
item.content:encoded: Looking for an Edgewonk alternative is usually not about Edgewonk being bad - it is about your needs changing. This is a fair comparison, not a takedown. Edgewonk is now an annual subscription of roughly $169 to $197/year (per edgewonk.com, accessed July 2026, not independently tested). It does market an MT4/MT5 Auto Sync, but per its own docs that is a periodic FTP sync of closed trades - it does not read open positions or live balance in real time. It has no walk-forward, and its Trade Simulator is a parametric what-if tool rather than a Monte Carlo that resamples your actual trade sequence. For prop firm traders that is the wrong tense: drawdown is enforced on live equity, so a closed-trade import is blind when a position is open and your headroom is on the line. We cover who should still use Edgewonk (desktop-first discretionary traders who value its deep tagging) and who should switch: MT4/MT5 and prop traders who want live open-position sync, real-time drawdown, and validation before paying an evaluation fee. SignalDeck keeps the R-multiple floor Edgewonk built and adds live sync plus Monte Carlo and walk-forward on top, with a Free tier so you can start without an annual commitment.

item.title: MT5 Trading Journal with Live Sync (Not EA Import)
item.description: Most MT5 journals sync through an installed Expert Advisor - closed trades only, no open positions, no live balance. A MetaApi session sees your account in real time. In a prop challenge, the connection method is the difference.
item.content:encoded: "We sync with MT5" can mean two very different things. An Expert Advisor is a script inside your terminal that writes trades out when they close - so it sees closed trades only, needs the terminal running, and never knows your live balance or open positions. SignalDeck connects through MetaApi instead: a broker-side session that reads your open positions and live account balance without an EA and without your terminal open. That matters because prop firm drawdown rules are evaluated on equity, including floating P and L - so a closed-trade log is blind at the exact moment a position is open and your headroom is on the line. This guide breaks down EA import vs a MetaApi session, why open-position visibility decides challenges, and what "live" honestly does and does not mean.

item.title: FTMO Trailing vs. Static Drawdown: The Reset Clock Trap
item.description: FTMO runs two formats with two different drawdown models. The 2-Step keeps a fixed floor; the 1-Step trails your highest closing balance and locks it in. Mix them up and you misjudge your headroom at the worst possible moment.
item.content:encoded: FTMO offers a 2-Step Challenge and a 1-Step Challenge, and their maximum-loss rules run on different clocks. The 2-Step uses a static 10% floor anchored to your initial balance, so profit banks real buffer. The 1-Step trails on an end-of-day basis, ratcheting the floor up to your highest closing balance and never back down - so a strong day can shrink the room you have left. This guide breaks down both models with worked $100K examples, the daily-limit reset clock, how the distinction changes position sizing, and what your journal must track for each.

item.title: Why Prop Firm Traders Keep Blowing Evaluations (And How to Stop It)

item.title: MAE and MFE: The Execution Metrics Most Traders Ignore
item.description:
